slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn to,
• Define what an **API** is using an analogy.
• Explain the purpose of an **API key**.
• Identify components of an **API** request.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

To follow this tutorial, you should have prior knowledge.
Refer to Module 2: Introduction to Prompting.

slides.title: What is an API? Think of it like a Restaurant Waiter.
slides.narration:
What is an **API**?
It stands for **Application Programming Interface**.
Think of it like a restaurant waiter.
Your app is the restaurant customer.
You want a dish from the kitchen, which is the **AI** model.
You give your order, or **prompt**, to the waiter.
The waiter, or **API**, takes your order to the kitchen.
The kitchen prepares your dish.
Then the waiter brings it back to you.
The **API** acts as a messenger between your application and an **AI** model.
slides.image_prompt: What is an API? Think of it like a Restaurant Waiter.

slides.title: What is an API Key? Think of it like your Restaurant ID Card.
slides.narration:
Now, what is an **API key**?
Think of it like your restaurant ID card.
An **API key** is a secret password.
It identifies you as an authorized user.
Just like an ID proves you can order food.
Your **API key** verifies your identity.
It ensures your interactions are secure and private.
You need it with each **API** request.
slides.image_prompt: What is an API Key? Think of it like your Restaurant ID Card.

slides.title: Real-Life Example: Checking Weather on Your Phone
slides.narration:
Let's see how this works in real life.
Open any weather app on your phone.
Tap the search bar to find a city.
Type your city name and press search.
Behind the scenes, the app sends a request to the **API**.
The weather **API** fetches data from sources.
It sends this data back to your app.
You now see the weather forecast on your screen.
This is an **API** in action!
slides.image_prompt: Real-Life Example: Checking Weather on Your Phone

slides.title: Making an API Request: Placing Your Order
slides.narration:
Making an **API** request is like placing your order.
You send your instructions to the **AI** model.
This 'order' has two main parts.
First, your **API key** for authentication.
This proves you are an authorized user.
Second, your **prompt** or instruction.
The **API** delivers this to the model.
The model processes it and sends a response.
slides.image_prompt: Making an API Request: Placing Your Order

slides.title: Demo: Vague Prompt Example
slides.narration:
Let's look at a vague **prompt** example.
Imagine you tell the **AI** model, 'Write a story'.
This is a very general request.
The **AI** will likely give you a generic story.
It might be uninspired and not what you want.

slides.title: Demo: Improved Prompt Example
slides.narration:
Now, let's try an improved **prompt**.
You could say, 'Write a short, exciting sci-fi story'.
Add more details like, 'about a space explorer'.
They discover a new alien species.
This happens on a barren planet.
This specific **prompt** guides the **AI**.
It helps generate a more engaging story.

slides.title: Demo: Vague vs. Improved Prompt Comparison
slides.narration:
Let us compare the outputs.
The vague **prompt** gave a generic story.
The improved **prompt** gave a focused story.
It resulted in a creative sci-fi adventure.
This shows the power of specific requests.
Clear details make a big difference.
slides.image_prompt: Demo: Vague vs. Improved Prompt Comparison

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined **APIs** using the waiter analogy.
We understood **API keys** as identification.
We explored **API** request components.
We also saw the impact of **prompt** quality.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
identify an **API** in another app you use daily.
Think about what the 'request' might be.
Also consider what 'response' the app receives.
Compare the results.
